en: Angry and bitter in speech or debate
hook: ACRIMONIOUS: ACRID, as bitter as acid.
story: Acrimonious. When Lamia's aunt and uncle divorced, nothing was peaceful. They shouted in the lawyer's office, insulted each other in court, and fought for months over every chair, spoon, and photograph. At family weddings, relatives seated them at opposite ends of the hall. The divorce was acrimonious: full of anger and bitterness. Acrid means sharp and bitter, like smoke. An acrimonious debate leaves both sides resentful long after it ends.

gre.s: What began as a friendly disagreement between the two scholars grew increasingly ____, until each was publicly accusing the other of fraud.
gre.clue: publicly accusing the other of fraud

en: Hostile and aggressive; eager to fight
hook: BELLI = war (rebellion). Ready for war.
story: Belligerent. At the bank, the queue moved slowly. One customer started muttering, then shouting, then slammed his fist on the counter and threatened to smash the glass if he was not served immediately. The terrified cashier pressed the alarm, and security guards escorted him out. He was belligerent: hostile, aggressive, eager to fight. Belli means war, as in rebellion. Belligerent nations are those at war. A belligerent tone turns any conversation into a battle.

gre.s: The diplomat's ____ remarks, which included open threats of military action, alarmed even his own government's allies.
gre.clue: open threats of military action

en: Doing good; generous and kind
hook: BENE = good, FIC = do. Doing good.
story: Beneficent. A businessman who grew up poor in a Kishoreganj village returned thirty years later as a millionaire. Quietly, he built three schools, a hospital, and a library. When the villagers wanted to name the buildings after him, he refused. "Name them after your mothers," he said. He was beneficent: actively doing good, generous and charitable. Bene means good, fic means do. Benevolent means wishing good; beneficent means actually doing it.

gre.s: The ____ foundation has funded clean-water projects in over forty countries, asking nothing in return from the communities it serves.
gre.clue: asking nothing in return from the communities it serves

en: Shrewd and careful, especially in money or business matters
hook: CANNY: like a CAN-do person who's never fooled.
story: Canny. Joya's grandmother is the most canny shopper in Kawran Bazar. She checks every tomato, knows the fair price of everything, notices when the scale is tilted, and bargains so skilfully that vendors lower their prices just to end the conversation. She has never been cheated in fifty years. She is canny: shrewd and careful, especially with money. Careful: uncanny means strange and mysterious, a completely different word.

gre.s: A ____ negotiator, she waited until the seller grew desperate before making her offer, securing the property far below its asking price.
gre.clue: waited until the seller grew desperate before making her offer

en: Showing arrogant or careless disregard for something important
hook: CAVALIER: a horse-riding knight who looks DOWN on everyone.
story: Cavalier. On the highway, a young driver weaved between buses at a hundred and twenty kilometres an hour. When a traffic officer stopped him and explained that he had nearly killed a family on a motorbike, the driver shrugged. "Nobody died, did they?" His attitude to safety was cavalier: arrogantly, carelessly dismissive of something important. A cavalier was a proud horseman who looked down on people on foot. A cavalier attitude toward deadlines gets you fired.

gre.s: Regulators criticized the company's ____ approach to safety, noting that it had ignored dozens of warnings from its own engineers.
gre.clue: had ignored dozens of warnings from its own engineers

en: Suffering from anxiety, sorrow, or pain; in serious difficulty
hook: DISTRESSED: under heavy STRESS.
story: Distressed. In the early morning, a fire swept through a row of shops in Mohammadpur. By sunrise, nothing remained of Rahima's tailoring shop but ashes and a melted sewing machine. She sat on the pavement, distressed and shaking, not knowing how she would feed her three children. Neighbours brought tea and sat beside her. Distressed means deeply upset, anxious, or in pain. In business, distressed companies are in serious financial difficulty.

gre.s: Hotline volunteers are trained to calm ____ callers, many of whom are panicking or in tears when they first phone in.
gre.clue: many of whom are panicking or in tears

en: Gradually becoming smaller or fewer
hook: DWINDLE: shrinking like a candle's WICK.
story: Dwindling. Two months before the GRE, Arif had saved fifteen thousand taka for the exam fee and food. Then the bills came: books, a laptop repair, transport to the test centre. Fifteen thousand became ten, then six, then three. He started cooking rice and eggs at home to make the last money last. His savings were dwindling: gradually becoming smaller. Dwindling forests, dwindling fish stocks, dwindling hope. Picture a candle burning lower each hour.

gre.s: Conservationists warn that the species' ____ population, now fewer than two hundred animals, may not survive another decade.
gre.clue: now fewer than two hundred animals

en: To overshadow; to surpass or make less important
hook: ECLIPSE: like the moon blocking out the sun.
story: Eclipse. Nadia was the family star: top of her class, debate champion, president of every club. Then her younger sister Priya started winning international math olympiads. Newspapers interviewed her. The prime minister shook her hand. At every family gathering, relatives only talked about Priya. Her fame had eclipsed Nadia's: overshadowed it, made it seem less important, like the moon blocking the sun. A new world record can eclipse an old one.

gre.s: Although the novelist was celebrated in her lifetime, her reputation came to ____ that of her more famous brother only after both had died.
gre.clue: her more famous brother

en: Comprehensive; covering a very wide range of knowledge
hook: ENCYCLOPEDIC: like an ENCYCLOPEDIA, knows everything.
story: Encyclopedic. Ask Rafi's uncle about any cricket match since 1985, and he will tell you the runs scored, the balls faced, the umpire's name, the weather, and what he ate while watching it. Last Eid, a cousin tried to stump him with an obscure question about a 1992 match in Sharjah. He answered in three seconds, with details. His cricket knowledge is encyclopedic: comprehensive, covering an enormous range of facts, like an encyclopedia.

gre.s: The guide's ____ knowledge of the city, extending from medieval architecture to the history of every street name, delighted the tourists.
gre.clue: extending from medieval architecture to the history of every street name

en: To make a bad situation worse
hook: EXACERBATE: EXTRA ACID on a wound.
story: Exacerbate. A mosquito bit Zayan's arm. It itched a little. He scratched. It itched more. He scratched harder. By evening, the tiny bite had become a red, swollen patch. Later, when his angry friend complained about something Zayan had said, Zayan shouted back, and the argument became a full fight. Both times he exacerbated the problem: made a bad situation worse. Exacerbate is the opposite of alleviate and mitigate. Think: extra acid on a wound.

gre.s: Rather than easing the shortage, the government's price controls only served to ____ it, as suppliers stopped selling at a loss.
gre.clue: Rather than easing the shortage

en: Intensely irritated and frustrated
hook: EXASPERATED: EX-ASP, bitten by a snake of annoyance.
story: Exasperated. Mitu explained the math problem to her little brother once. He nodded. She asked him to solve it. He could not. She explained again, slower. Again. With drawings. With apples. After the fifth time, when he asked, "Wait, what is a fraction?", she threw her hands in the air. She was exasperated: intensely irritated and frustrated, especially after repeated problems. Exasperation is the feeling of reaching the end of your patience.

gre.s: After the airline cancelled his flight for the third time in a week, the ____ traveler finally gave up and rented a car.
gre.clue: for the third time in a week

en: Interchangeable; replaceable by another identical item
hook: FUNGIBLE: FUN to swap, since one is as good as another.
story: Fungible. If Sara lends you a hundred-taka note and you return a different hundred-taka note, she does not mind. Any note is as good as another. But if she lends you her grandmother's wedding ring, you cannot return a different ring, however similar. Money is fungible: interchangeable with any identical item. The ring is not. Rice, oil, and gold are fungible. Artworks, memories, and people are not.

gre.s: Unlike works of art, which are unique, commodities such as wheat are ____: one bushel can be substituted for another without any loss of value.
gre.clue: one bushel can be substituted for another without any loss of value

en: Overused and therefore lacking significance; unoriginal
hook: HACKNEYED: like an old HACK horse, used until worn out.
story: Hackneyed. The new film began: a poor village boy meets a rich city girl. Her father disapproves. They sing a song in the rain. They dance in Switzerland. The father relents at the hospital. Viewers in the cinema mouthed the dialogue before the actors spoke. The plot was hackneyed: so overused that it had lost all freshness and meaning. A hackney was an old hired horse, worked until it was worn out. Synonyms: trite, banal.

gre.s: Students were warned that the examiners would penalize ____ openings such as "since the dawn of time," which appear in thousands of essays every year.
gre.clue: which appear in thousands of essays every year

en: Out of place; not in harmony with the surroundings
hook: IN-CONGRUOUS: not CONGRUENT, doesn't match.
story: Incongruous. In the middle of a muddy village road, beside a tea stall with a tin roof and goats grazing nearby, sat a gleaming red Ferrari, its owner visiting his grandmother. Children gathered around it in amazement. It looked like a spaceship had landed in a rice field. The car was incongruous: out of place, not in harmony with its surroundings. On the GRE, an author might notice something incongruous in an argument.

gre.s: The modern glass tower looks strangely ____ among the medieval stone buildings that surround it.
gre.clue: among the medieval stone buildings that surround it

en: Able to be swapped with each other without difference
hook: INTER-CHANGE-able: can be CHANGED between.
story: Interchangeable. Nadia's phone charger broke. She grabbed her brother's from his desk, and it fit perfectly. Their chargers were interchangeable: able to replace each other without any difference. In everyday English, "big" and "large" are usually interchangeable. But on the GRE, many words that seem similar are not interchangeable: "complacent" and "confident," for example, mean very different things. Interchangeable is a close synonym of fungible.

gre.s: Though the two terms are often treated as ____, scientists use them to describe quite different phenomena.
gre.clue: scientists use them to describe quite different phenomena

en: Using very few words; brief and to the point
hook: LACONIC: LACKS words, just the minimum.
story: Laconic. Arif rehearsed for two days before asking his strict father for permission to study abroad. He prepared statistics, a budget, and three emotional speeches. He began nervously. His father listened for thirty seconds, put down his newspaper, and said four words: "Go. Study hard. Call." Then he returned to his paper. His reply was laconic: using very few words, brief and to the point. Laconia was a region of ancient Greece famous for short speeches.

gre.s: Unlike his famously verbose predecessor, the new chairman was ____, often answering complex questions with a single sentence.
gre.clue: often answering complex questions with a single sentence

en: Producing a great deal of profit
hook: LUCRATIVE: brings in lots of LUCRE (money).
story: Lucrative. In his second year at university, Rafi started designing websites for small businesses in his spare time. First for a cousin's bakery, then a friend's clothing shop, then a hotel in Cox's Bazar. Within a year, he was earning more than his father's government salary, from his bedroom. His freelance business had become lucrative: highly profitable. Lucre is an old word for money. Software engineering and medicine are often lucrative careers.

gre.s: Many talented scientists abandon research for more ____ careers in finance, where salaries can be ten times higher.
gre.clue: where salaries can be ten times higher

en: Having or showing great authority; sometimes domineering
hook: MAGISTERIAL: like a MAGISTRATE in court.
story: Magisterial. When Professor Ahmed entered the lecture hall, students stopped whispering immediately. He spoke slowly and with total certainty, never once looking at notes, and nobody dared interrupt. His thousand-page history of Bengal is considered the definitive work, quoted by every scholar. Both his manner and his book are magisterial: showing great authority. Sometimes magisterial suggests a domineering tone. Picture a magistrate in court, commanding the whole room.

gre.s: The historian's ____ survey of the empire, which drew on sources in twelve languages, is still regarded as the definitive work on the subject.
gre.clue: is still regarded as the definitive work

en: Involving heavy, burdensome effort
hook: ONEROUS: a heavy ONUS (burden).
story: Onerous. When his father passed away, twenty-four-year-old Tanvir became the head of the family. He paid for his mother's medicine, his two sisters' university fees, the rent, and his grandmother's care, all on a junior bank officer's salary. He worked weekends and gave private tuition at night. The responsibility was onerous: heavy and burdensome. An onus is a burden. Onerous duties, onerous taxes, onerous regulations all weigh you down.

gre.s: Small businesses complained that the new regulations were so ____ that compliance alone would consume most of their profits.
gre.clue: compliance alone would consume most of their profits

en: Harsh public criticism or disgrace
hook: OPPROBRIUM: OPPOSITE of APPROBATION (praise).
story: Opprobrium. After a factory building collapsed and killed hundreds of workers, investigators revealed that its owners had ignored cracks in the walls and forced people to return to work. The public's reaction was furious: protests, angry headlines, international condemnation. The owners could not leave their homes. They faced opprobrium: harsh public criticism and disgrace. Opprobrium is the opposite of approbation, which means approval. Both are formal GRE words.

gre.s: The athlete, once a national hero, faced public ____ after the doping scandal, with sponsors abandoning him and fans burning his jersey.
gre.clue: sponsors abandoning him and fans burning his jersey

en: Extremely unwilling to spend money; stingy
hook: PARSIMONIOUS: PARSING every penny, unwilling to spend.
story: Parsimonious. Uncle Kamal is rich. But he reuses tea bags three times, refuses to turn on the ceiling fan in summer, walks forty minutes to save a ten-taka rickshaw fare, and gives his grandchildren exactly two taka each on Eid. When his son asked for money for medicine, he asked for receipts first. He is parsimonious: extremely unwilling to spend money, stingy. Think: parsing every penny. It is the opposite of prodigal and extravagant.

gre.s: The billionaire was so ____ that he installed pay phones in his mansion so that guests would have to pay for their own calls.
gre.clue: installed pay phones in his mansion

en: Of minor importance; on the edge or outer part
hook: PERIPHERAL: on the PERIMETER, at the edge.
story: Peripheral. In the GRE reading passage, the author spent one paragraph describing her childhood in a fishing village. Lamia wasted three minutes re-reading it. Then the questions came, and none of them asked about the village; they were all about the main argument on climate policy. The childhood story had been peripheral: of minor importance, at the edge of the main topic. Your peripheral vision sees what is at the edges. Focus on the centre.

gre.s: The committee dismissed the objection as ____, since it concerned the project's color scheme rather than its safety or cost.
gre.clue: rather than its safety or cost

en: Causing a strong reaction, especially anger or interest; deliberately stimulating
hook: PROVOCATIVE: it PROVOKES you.
story: Provocative. On the first day of his ethics class, Professor Haque wrote one question on the board: "Is it ever morally right to cheat?" Then he sat down and waited. Within five minutes, the class had divided into two camps, voices rising, hands waving, students who never spoke now shouting arguments. His question was provocative: deliberately causing a strong reaction, whether anger or interest. A provocative statement provokes you to respond.

gre.s: The museum's ____ exhibit, featuring images designed to shock, drew both furious protests and record crowds.
gre.clue: featuring images designed to shock

en: To formally give up a claim, right, or belief
hook: RE-NOUNCE: an annouNCEment that you're giving it up.
story: Renounce. Over two thousand five hundred years ago, a young prince in Nepal had everything: palaces, jewels, a beautiful wife. One night, he left it all behind, gave away his fine clothes, and walked into the forest as a wandering monk. He became the Buddha. He had renounced his royal life: formally given it up. To renounce is to abandon a claim, right, belief, or possession. Synonyms: abjure, forswear, relinquish.

gre.s: To accept the post, the businessman was required to ____ his foreign citizenship and divest himself of all private holdings.
gre.clue: divest himself of all private holdings

en: Full of strong, turbulent emotions; stormy
hook: TEMPESTUOUS: like a TEMPEST (violent storm).
story: Tempestuous. The two famous painters fell in love in Paris. Their relationship was legendary: wild declarations of love one week, slammed doors and broken plates the next. They separated four times and married twice. Friends never knew whether to buy them a wedding gift or a sympathy card. Their love was tempestuous: stormy, full of strong, turbulent emotions. A tempest is a violent storm at sea. Tempestuous weather, a tempestuous temper.

gre.s: The composer's ____ relationship with his patron, marked by violent quarrels and tearful reconciliations, inspired several of his most passionate works.
gre.clue: marked by violent quarrels and tearful reconciliations

en: Able to be defended or maintained against criticism
hook: TENABLE: can be held (tenere, to hold). An argument that holds up.
story: Tenable. For forty years, Professor Karim taught that a certain fish species could not survive in salty water. Then a student brought him new data: thousands of the fish, thriving in the Sundarbans' brackish rivers. The old professor studied the evidence for a week, then stood before his class. "My position is no longer tenable." Tenable means able to be defended against criticism. Tenere means to hold. An untenable situation cannot continue.

gre.s: Once the new fossil evidence emerged, the theory that birds evolved separately from dinosaurs was no longer ____.
gre.clue: Once the new fossil evidence emerged

en: An act that violates a rule, law, or moral code
hook: TRANS-GRESS: stepping ACROSS (trans) the line.
story: Transgression. The national team's best bowler was caught on camera scratching the ball with a bottle cap to make it swing. He apologized and cried at the press conference, but the cricket board banned him for a full year. His transgression shocked fans who had idolized him. A transgression is an act that violates a rule, law, or moral code. Trans means across, gress means step: stepping across the line. Small transgressions can grow into big ones.

gre.s: The senator's minor ____, a forgotten parking fine, was seized upon by opponents eager to portray him as contemptuous of the law.
gre.clue: a forgotten parking fine

en: Polished, sophisticated, and courteous
hook: URBANE: URBAN, city-polished manners.
story: Urbane. At the diplomatic dinner, the ambassador moved gracefully from guest to guest, switching effortlessly between English, French, Arabic, and Bangla. He remembered every name, told witty stories, and when a guest insulted his country, he smiled and replied with polite charm. Nobody could ruffle him. He was urbane: polished, sophisticated, and courteous, like a refined city dweller. Urbane shares a root with urban. Its opposite is boorish or uncouth.

gre.s: The ____ host, polished and witty, put even his most awkward guests at ease.
gre.clue: polished and witty

en: The appearance of being true or real
hook: VERI-SIMILI-TUDE: VERY SIMILAR to truth.
story: Verisimilitude. To make a film about the 1971 war, the director filmed in real villages, dressed actors in authentic uniforms, used weapons from the period, and hired old freedom fighters as advisers. When veterans watched the premiere, several of them cried. "That is exactly how it was," one said. The film had verisimilitude: the quality of appearing true or real. Veri means true, simili means similar. Good novels have verisimilitude even when invented.

gre.s: The novel's historical details lend it a striking ____, though every one of its characters is invented.
gre.clue: though every one of its characters is invented

en: To spoil or impair the quality or effectiveness of
hook: VITIATE: makes it VICIOUS, corrupts it.
story: Vitiate. For six months, Ishita's research team ran an experiment on plant growth. Then they discovered that one thermometer had been broken from the start, showing the wrong temperature every single day. Every result became unreliable. Six months of work was useless. The faulty thermometer had vitiated the experiment: spoiled its quality and effectiveness. A single lie can vitiate a friendship; bias can vitiate research. Synonyms: impair, corrupt.

gre.s: A single undisclosed conflict of interest can ____ an otherwise rigorous study, rendering its conclusions suspect.
gre.clue: rendering its conclusions suspect
